To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) Si intervention in rats increased serum and tissue Si levels, (ii) the increase was more marked in female rats, (iii) serum Si levels correlated with BMD, and (iv) the association was stronger for females than males.

1) silicon is a trace element in the diet, 2) silicon is found in bone, 3) silicon is found at high concentrations in the bloodstream of rats, 4) silicon supplementation increased silicon concentrations in blood and bone, 5) bone quality was improved in rats that had received silicon supplementation.

(i) serum Si concentrations were positively associated with bone mineral density in young female rats following oral Si supplementation with monometyl-silanetriol; and (ii) this association was absent in male rats and was not mediated by bone Si content.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms of action of silicon in relation to bone and the potential for Si to be developed as a therapeutic agent for osteoporosis.
the role of dietary silicon in bone health and the mechanisms underlying this effect.
the role of dietary silicon in the maintenance of bone health and in particular, the role of silicon in the prevention and/or treatment of osteoporosis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
silicon supplementation in female rats increases serum Si levels and osteocalcin concentration, and this may increase BMD, which is associated with increased serum Si level.
silicon is a beneficial nutrient to support bone health in women.
Si supplementation in rats increases serum Si levels and that these levels are associated with bone mineral density in females.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Si supplementation increases serum Si levels, which in turn increases osteocalcin levels and BMD in females.
silicon supplementation increases circulating estradiol levels and that this effect is associated with increased bone quality in female rats.
the Si-estradiols interaction is a systemic effect that is mediated through the liver and not through the incorporation of Si into bone.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Si effect in bone is not due to Si per se, but rather to its interaction with estrogen, and this is mediated by Si in the blood, rather than in bone.
the Si effect on bone quality in younger females may be due, at least in part, to an interaction between Si and estradiol.
the positive association between serum silicon and BMD may be mediated by serum estradiol level.
